content: The International Association for Hospice and Palliative Care and other relevant non-governmental organizations (NGOs) not officially affiliated with the World Health Organization (WHO), as well as donors, potential donors, publishers of translated versions, and contributors to the development of these guidelines, have been acknowledged. Invitations to conferences to discuss and present the guidelines will be accepted when feasible. Additionally, the publication of novel developments emerging from systematic reviews in peer-reviewed journals will be considered. The guidelines aim to be accessible in all official WHO languages, and NGOs in official relations with WHO will be encouraged to support their translation as part of their work plans with WHO. Translations into non-United Nations languages and publications in these languages by third parties will also be encouraged. These guidelines are intended to serve as the first in a series of clinical guidelines addressing symptom management in palliative care. They will also contribute to the growing body of guidance on pain management. Implementation of the guidelines will be supported through WHO regional and country offices. Ongoing cancer control and palliative care programs will be provided with the new guidelines, which will also be integrated into palliative care training programs and curricula. The implementation of the guidelines will be evaluated after dissemination, with the understanding that their adoption depends more on the regulatory frameworks of individual countries than on the willingness to use the guidelines. A key goal of the guidelines is to foster a policy environment conducive to the development of balanced national policies for the use of controlled essential medications. Metrics such as the number of downloads from the WHO website, sales of printed copies, and third-party translations will serve as indicators of the guidelines' dissemination and impact. For local adaptations, WHO encourages potential users to contact the relevant WHO focal point for resources to aid in tailoring the guidelines to specific localities. A user-feedback questionnaire will be distributed one year after the initial publication to evaluate the guidelines. The systematic review team, led by Dr. Ethan Balk from the Brown Center for Evidence Synthesis in Health at Brown University, conducted literature searches, assessed the eligibility of systematic reviews and primary studies, extracted data, evaluated the risk of bias, and performed pairwise meta-analyses. The network meta-analysis team, led by Dr. Georgia Salanti from the University of Bern, developed outputs to inform the Guideline Development Group (GDG) recommendations using GRADE methodology. Dr. Nandi Siegfried served as the guideline methodologist. External observers from various organizations, including the International Association for Hospice and Palliative Care, the Worldwide Hospice and Palliative Care Alliance, and others, provided input during the scoping of the guidelines. The WHO Guideline Steering Group, led by Dr. Cherian Varghese, oversaw the technical aspects of the guidelines' development. The GDG members, representing diverse regions and expertise, disclosed their interests, which were reviewed for potential conflicts. WHO policies on conflicts of interest were strictly applied, and any significant conflicts were managed appropriately. Members with potential conflicts were excluded from certain aspects of the guideline development process. The guidelines' publication includes a detailed account of the declared conflicts and the strategies employed to manage them. Annex 5 provides an overview of the rules governing the procurement, distribution, and dispensing of opioid medicines, as well as their status as controlled substances under the United Nations Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961. This annex is intended to guide policymakers and managers in ensuring appropriate access to these medications.
